entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

Exit the plugin when its dispatcher dies

A SIGKILLed entire CLI cannot forward anything to this plugin: the
plugin reparents to pid 1 and holds locks/write.lock until it finishes,
so every concurrent reader fails brain_locked. Hook runners commonly
escalate to SIGKILL on timeout, which is how a customer hit this.

Arm an event-driven parent-death watchdog in cli.Execute: one goroutine
blocks on the platform's parent-exit event (kqueue NOTE_EXIT on darwin,
pidfd+poll on linux with a PDEATHSIG fallback for kernels before 5.3,
WaitForSingleObject on windows) and exits the process when it fires. No
timers. A ppid re-check after registration closes the race where the
parent dies first. Immediate exit is safe: store writes are atomic
renames and flocks release on process exit.

Exemptions: a process whose initial ppid is 1 (launchd/systemd daemon)
never arms, and spawnDetached now sets ENTIRE_BRAIN_DETACHED=1 on every
child it starts. Setting the marker centrally matters because the
daemon-reregister child's parent is killed by launchctl bootout by
design; arming it would abort re-registration at the exact moment it
must survive.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
)" && git log --oneline -1 && git push -u origin evisdren/ywbn5 2>&1 | tail -2

entire trail create --type bug --title "Exit the entire-brain plugin when its dispatcher dies" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Why

A customer runs many agents against one shared brain. Their prompt hook killed `entire brain facts promote` after 4 seconds with SIGKILL. SIGKILL to the `entire` CLI cannot be forwarded, so the plugin child reparented to pid 1 and held `locks/write.lock` for its full runtime (20 s to 1.5 min). Every concurrent reader failed `brain_locked`. SIGTERM was already covered by forwarding; SIGKILL was the gap.

## What changed

- New package `internal/cli/internal/parentwatch`. `Arm()` (called from `cli.Execute`) starts one goroutine that blocks on an OS parent-exit event and calls `os.Exit(1)` with one stderr line when it fires. No timers, no polling. Platform watchers: kqueue `NOTE_EXIT` (darwin), `pidfd_open` + `poll` with a `PR_SET_PDEATHSIG` fallback for kernels before 5.3 (linux), `OpenProcess` + `WaitForSingleObject` (windows).
- A ppid re-check after registration closes the race where the parent dies before the watcher exists; it also covers registration errors such as ESRCH.
- Exemptions: no arming when initial ppid is 1 (launchd/systemd daemon), and no arming when `ENTIRE_BRAIN_DETACHED=1` is set. `spawnDetached` sets that marker on every child it starts. Central placement matters: `relaunchInstalledDaemon` spawns `daemon-reregister` through `spawnDetached`, and that child's parent is killed by `launchctl bootout` by design — arming it would abort re-registration exactly when it must survive.
- On any watcher failure with a live parent, `Arm` degrades to no watchdog. It never kills a process whose parent is alive.

Immediate exit is safe: store writes are atomic renames and flocks release on process exit. An aborted mutation loses only its batch.

## Validation

- Unit tests for the arming rules; an integration test re-execs the test binary as parent and armed child, SIGKILLs the parent, and asserts the child exits well under a second and its flock is released (5 repeated runs, clean).
- `go test ./internal/cli ./internal/cli/internal/parentwatch` green (247 s / 0.6 s).
- `gofmt -l -s` and `go vet` clean; cross-compiles for linux, windows, and freebsd (no-op fallback) pass.

## Known limits

- A command that spawned a coding-agent child orphans it on watchdog exit — identical to today's SIGKILL behavior, so no regression. The customer's failing command (`facts promote`) spawns no subprocesses.
- The PDEATHSIG fallback tracks the parent thread, not strictly the process (documented in the code).
- Dispatcher-side `Pdeathsig` on the plugin spawn (entire CLI repo) would be defense in depth; separate task.

Recorded design decision: Brain fact `fact:9c49fbb9132406a0a692e857` (branch `evisdren/brain_locked-write.lock-fix`); the full four-cause customer diagnosis is `fact:1d10ce176f39425716a28b6e`.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF
)" --json 2>&1 | tail -30

# Review PR

Review a pull request with structured, actionable feedback.

## Arguments

- `this PR and then implement any fixes that come from it. also note that there is a finding on a trail that needs to be resolved.` — PR number, URL, or branch name. If empty, review the current branch's open PR.

## Process

### 1. Fetch PR context

```
gh pr view <pr> --json title,body,baseRefName,headRefName,additions,deletions,changedFiles,commits,author
gh pr diff <pr>
```

Read the PR description carefully — it defines scope and intent. Everything you review should be evaluated against what the PR is trying to accomplish.

### 2. Understand the change

Before reviewing line-by-line:
- What is this PR doing and why?
- What files are touched and what's the blast radius?
- Are there any architectural implications?

### 3. Review with this checklist

**Correctness**
- Does the code do what the PR description says?
- Are there logic errors, off-by-one bugs, or unhandled edge cases?
- Are error paths handled correctly?

**Security**
- Any injection risks (SQL, XSS, command injection)?
- Are secrets, tokens, or credentials handled safely?
- Are inputs validated at system boundaries?

**Testing**
- Are there tests for the new/changed behavior?
- Do tests cover edge cases, not just the happy path?
- Are test assertions meaningful (not just "doesn't throw")?

**Design**
- Does the change follow existing codebase patterns and conventions?
- Is the abstraction level appropriate (not over/under-engineered)?
- Are there unnecessary changes outside the stated scope?

**Performance**
- Any N+1 queries, unbounded loops, or missing pagination?
- Are there opportunities for batching or caching that were missed?
- Will this scale with the data sizes it will encounter?

**Readability**
- Are names clear and consistent with the codebase?
- Is complex logic adequately explained?
- Would a future reader understand the "why" behind non-obvious decisions?

### 4. Adversarial review

Take a second, adversarial pass over the diff. Actively try to break the change — assume it has flaws and hunt for them across:

- **Performance** — worst-case inputs, hot paths, allocations, contention.
- **Stability** — race conditions, partial failures, retries, resource leaks, crash recovery.
- **Correctness** — inputs and states that violate the author's assumptions.
- **Simplicity** — code that could be deleted or replaced with something simpler/stdlib.
- **Platform design standards** — deviations from the platform's established design patterns and conventions.

Add any findings to the output using the same severity format.

### 5. Run /simplify

Run the `/simplify` skill (via the Skill tool) against the changed code and fold its findings into the review output.

### 6. Structure your output

For each finding, use this format:

**[severity] file:line — short title**
Description of the issue and why it matters. Include a suggested fix when possible.

Severity levels:
- **[blocking]** — Must fix before merge. Correctness bugs, security issues, data loss risks.
- **[important]** — Should fix. Design problems, missing tests for critical paths, performance issues.
- **[nit]** — Nice to fix. Style, naming, minor improvements. Don't block merge on these.
- **[question]** — Not necessarily wrong, but needs clarification or discussion.

### 7. Summary

End with a brief summary:
- Overall assessment (approve / request changes / needs discussion)
- What the PR does well
- Top 1-3 items that need attention
- Any scope concerns (changes that seem unrelated to the stated goal)

## Guidelines

- Review what's in the diff, not what you wish was there. Don't request unrelated refactoring.
- If the PR is large, focus on the most impactful files first.
- Be specific — "this could be better" is not useful. Show what "better" looks like.
- Distinguish between "this is wrong" and "I would do this differently." Only the former is blocking.
- If you're unsure about something, use [question] severity instead of asserting it's wrong.
- Read relevant source files (not just the diff) when you need context about how changed code integrates with the rest of the system.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/evisdrenova/.claude/plugins/cache/entire-skills/entire/0.7.2/skills/address-findings

# Address Findings

Fix and resolve the open review findings on an Entire trail. A finding is a
review comment posted to a trail on entire.io: it has a file/line location, a
body, a severity, and sometimes a suggested unified-diff patch. This skill
fetches the open findings, applies or hand-fixes each one in the current
worktree, and marks it resolved on the trail.

## When to use / not use

Use when the user points at a trail — a URL like
`https://<host>/<forge>/<owner>/<repo>/trails/<number>/<slug>`, or a bare trail
number or branch — and asks to **address / fix / resolve** its findings or
review comments.

Do **not** use this skill for:

- A code review of the current diff — that is the `review` skill (read-only).
- Creating new findings — use `entire trail finding add`.

## Response Format

Begin the first response to this skill invocation with the line:

`Entire Address Findings:`

followed by a blank line, then the content. Apply the header to the **first
response only**. Omit it on error / early-exit responses (CLI missing, not
authenticated, trail not found, branch mismatch, no open findings).

## Rules

1. Make the smallest correct change that addresses each finding. Do not expand scope.
2. Only mark a finding resolved when you actually addressed it. If a finding is
   ambiguous or needs a human decision, leave it open and report it.
3. Do not commit or push. Leave changes in the working tree for the user to review.
4. Never weaken a test or assertion just to clear a finding.

## Process

### 1. Verify the CLI

Run `entire version`. If the command is not found, stop and tell the user:
"The Entire CLI is required but not installed. Install it from
https://entire.io/docs/cli and try again."

### 2. Resolve the trail selector

- If the argument is a trail URL, take the number from the `/trails/<number>/`
  path segment and use that number.
- If it is a bare trail number, id, or branch name, use it as-is.
- If you cannot determine a trail, stop and ask the user for the trail URL or number.

Use this value as the `<trail>` selector for every command below. `entire trail`
accepts a trail number, id, or branch name interchangeably, so no number lookup
is needed — a branch name works directly.

### 3. Fetch open findings

```bash
entire trail finding list <trail> --json --status open
```

- If the output reports that authentication is required, stop and tell the user:
  "`entire trail finding list` requires authentication. Run `entire login` and try again."
- If the `trail finding` subcommand is unavailable, or the API reports the
  feature is not enabled, stop and tell the user that trail findings may not be
  enabled for this account or repository. Do not invent findings.
- Parse the JSON. Each finding has an id, a severity, a status, a body, a
  location (file path + line range), and may include a suggested change (a
  unified diff).
- If there are no open findings, report "No open findings on this trail." and stop.

### 4. Branch guard (you must be on the trail's branch)

`entire trail finding apply` edits the local worktree, so you must be on the
trail's branch before changing files.

```bash
git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD                # current branch
entire trail list --json --status any -n 200   # locate the trail's branch
```

Find the trail whose `number` or `branch` matches your selector and read its `branch`.

- If the trail's branch differs from the current branch, stop and tell the user:
  "Trail `<trail>` targets branch `<trail-branch>`, but you are on
  `<current-branch>`. Check it out first (`entire trail checkout <trail>`) and
  re-run." Do not edit files.
- If you cannot find the trail in the list (e.g. pagination), do not hard-fail:
  warn that you could not verify the branch, and ask the user to confirm they are
  on the trail's branch before you continue.

### 5. Address each finding

Process findings highest severity first (high → medium → low). For each:

1. **If it has a suggested unified-diff change**, dry-run it first:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding apply <trail> <finding-id> --check
   ```

   If it applies cleanly, apply and resolve in one step:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding apply <trail> <finding-id> --resolve
   ```

2. **Otherwise** (no patch, the patch conflicts, or the fix needs reasoning):
   read the finding body, open the file at its location, and make the smallest
   correct edit that addresses it. If a fast, relevant local check exists for the
   touched code (a build or a focused test), run it. Then resolve:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding resolve <trail> <finding-id> -m "<one line: what you changed>"
   ```

3. **If you cannot confidently address it** (ambiguous, needs a product/design
   decision, or out of scope): leave it open, do not resolve it, and record it
   for the report.

### 6. Report

Summarize:

- Resolved via suggested patch — list finding ids and files.
- Resolved via manual edit — list finding ids, files, and a one-line of what changed.
- Left open for your decision — list finding ids and why.
- Any errors encountered.

Remind the user the changes are uncommitted and ready for review.

## Failure modes

- **CLI not installed** → install message (step 1).
- **Not authenticated** → "`entire trail finding list` requires authentication. Run `entire login` and try again."
- **Trail findings not enabled / API error** → tell the user the feature may be
  unavailable; do not fabricate findings.
- **Trail not found** → tell the user to check the URL or number; suggest
  `entire trail list --status any`.
- **Wrong branch** → stop with the checkout instruction (step 4).
- **Patch does not apply** → fall back to a manual edit; if you cannot fix it
  confidently, leave the finding open and report it.
- **Not a git repository** → stop and tell the user to run from inside the trail's repo.

There's already an open PR #584, probably opened by trail creation or Conductor. Its one open finding (low severity, confidence 0.4) says the PDEATHSIG fallback should also handle EPERM and other PidfdOpen errors, not just ENOSYS. I'll check that claim before acting on it, since in containers with seccomp filtering pidfd_open can return EPERM.

I'm weighing whether the PDEATHSIG fallback should cover any PidfdOpen error rather than only ENOSYS. EPERM from seccomp is plausible, and prctl PR_SET_PDEATHSIG is old and broadly allowed, so a fallback looks safe. If the parent has already died and PidfdOpen returns ESRCH, the ppid recheck after the fallback should still catch it.

I'm reviewing the open finding now, and before going further I want to confirm its premise about EPERM. Falling back to PDEATHSIG on any PidfdOpen error looks sound, since prctl is old and broadly permitted, and the ppid recheck still covers the case where the parent has already died. Next I'll go through the diff for correctness and edge cases.

Next I'm checking the env handling in spawnDetached: the appended ENTIRE_BRAIN_DETACHED marker should win over any earlier value because os/exec keeps the last entry. The backfill child then inherits that marker, so nested entire-brain calls underneath it won't try to arm again.

content.text:
`/simplify → 4 cleanup agents in parallel → apply the fixes`

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change fixes the root cause at the right depth rather than
patching a symptom with a fragile bandaid. Special cases layered on shared
infrastructure are a sign the fix isn't deep enough — prefer the simpler, more
general change to the underlying mechanism over adding special cases, and name
that change.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).

<result>Not clean. Arming in `cli.Execute` is the right layer, but the detached exemption is too narrow: it lives in one spawn helper when it should follow what "detached" means.

**1. The marker covers one detach path, but the codebase has two.** (`internal/cli/setup_spawn.go:37-44` and `internal/cli/memory_cmd.go:129`)
- `launchDetachedSelf` is a second detach primitive. It is used by `memory notify` (`memory_cmd.go:124` and `memory_notify_sync.go:30`) to start a `memory worker --once` that is meant to outlive the short-lived notify process. Its own comment says "if this process exits first, the child is reparented and keeps running".
- It doesn't go through `spawnDetached`, so it never gets `ENTIRE_BRAIN_DETACHED=1`. With `cli.Execute` now arming the watchdog for every process, that worker is exposed to it.
- The marker is also an inherited environment variable. Any `entire-brain` process started from inside a detached child, such as a backfill re-exec, inherits it and skips the watchdog. That is the same orphan risk one level down.
- In short, the exemption is tied to "called through `spawnDetached`" rather than to "this process was deliberately detached".

**2. Session leadership is the deeper mechanism, and the code already relies on it.** (`internal/cli/internal/parentwatch/parentwatch.go:20` and `internal/cli/setup_spawn_unix.go:12`)
- On Unix, `spawnDetached` already makes the child a session leader with `Setsid: true`. launchd and systemd jobs are also session leaders.
- A check like `unix.Getsid(0) == os.Getpid()` in `shouldArm` would cover both current exemptions (initial ppid 1 and the marker) with one fact the OS reports. Unlike an environment variable, it doesn't pass down to grandchildren.
- `launchDetachedSelf` should then use `detachedSysProcAttr()` too, so both detach paths share one definition of "detached" and both are exempt.
- The environment marker would only be needed on Windows, where `CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP` can't be checked from inside the child.

**3. Arming in `cli.Execute` and handling this at the process level are both right.** (`internal/cli/root.go:50` and `internal/cli/internal/brainstore/filelock.go:45,172`)
- Whether `entire` dispatched this process is a property of the process, not of a command. Arming per command would repeat the call in every verb that takes the lock.
- The lock layer has nothing that would solve this more generally. `BrainWriteLockTimeout` (10s) only limits how long other processes wait for the lock, not how long the holder keeps it. There is no lease, and the kernel already releases `flock`/`LockFileEx` when the holder dies.
- So ending the orphaned process is the correct fix, not a duplicate of an existing mechanism.</result>

I'm checking the reuse findings: adopting `clitest.PinXDGRoots(m)` in the TestMain default branch since it's the package convention and keeps XDG hermetic. I still need to confirm its signature, which I expect returns an exit code. I'm keeping my own helper-subprocess TestMain approach, since helpers have to run without normal test flag parsing.

I'm weighing whether to adopt `brainstore.ProcessAlive` in the parentwatch tests. The import is safe since the packages are siblings with no cycle, and the file is unix-only, which fits the darwin/linux test build. Its kill-with-signal-0 check has the same zombie caveat as my ESRCH check, so for consistency I'm leaning toward reusing it.

I'm going to use `brainstore.AcquireFileLock` in the integration test rather than raw flock, so the test exercises the real lock that had the write.lock release bug. The child will hold the lock, and after it dies the test should be able to acquire it again with a zero timeout. I still need to confirm the function's signature and that contention returns `ErrFileLockTimeout`.

Still settling on the env handling: `cmd.Environ()` can replace the hand-rolled env merge, and duplicates resolve in favor of later entries either way. I'm skipping the `EnvBool` change, since the marker is an internal spawn contract and pulling in the base package would drag the tui dependency into parentwatch. Next I'll apply two fixes: a PDEATHSIG fallback on any `PidfdOpen` error, and a bool return from `wait()`.

Next I'm sketching a shared helper for the unix build so the darwin and linux wait loops don't duplicate each other. The kqueue version returns true on any event and false on a real error. If the call returns zero events with no error, I'll treat that as a degrade rather than spin.

I'm working through the remaining items: a shared wait helper so the darwin and linux loops don't duplicate the EINTR and degrade logic, switching the spawn env to `cmd.Environ()`, and changing `shouldArm` to take the ppid and detached value directly. I also need to add the three test adoptions (`PinXDGRoots`, `ProcessAlive`, `AcquireFileLock`), rewrite the PR title and body while keeping the shadow marker, and resolve the trail finding after verifying. The EPERM fallback can't be tested on darwin without injection, so I'll note it and skip a test, keeping the suite green throughout.

gh pr edit 584 --title "Exit the plugin when its dispatcher dies" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
<!-- entire-shadow-pr -->

Trail: https://entire.com/gh/entireio/-/trails/2715 (findings and review live there)

## Why

SIGTERM to the `entire` CLI is forwarded to this plugin, but SIGKILL cannot be: the plugin reparents to pid 1 and holds `locks/write.lock` until it finishes (20 s–1.5 min for `facts promote`), failing every concurrent reader with `brain_locked`. Hook runners commonly escalate to SIGKILL on timeout; a customer hit exactly this.

## What

- `internal/cli/internal/parentwatch`: `Arm()` (called from `cli.Execute`) registers an OS parent-exit watch synchronously, then one goroutine blocks on it and exits the process when the parent is gone. kqueue `NOTE_EXIT` (darwin), `pidfd_open`+`poll` (linux, with `PR_SET_PDEATHSIG` fallback on any `pidfd_open` failure — ENOSYS on kernels < 5.3, EPERM under seccomp), `WaitForSingleObject` (windows). No timers. A ppid re-check after registration closes the parent-died-first race.
- The wait reports true only for an observed parent exit; registration or wait failures with a live parent degrade to no watchdog. It can never kill a process whose parent is alive.
- Exemptions: initial ppid 1 (launchd/systemd daemons), and `ENTIRE_BRAIN_DETACHED=1`, set by both detach paths — `spawnDetached` (setup backfill, `daemon-reregister`, whose parent dies by design under `launchctl bootout`) and `launchDetachedSelf` (memory workers, which must outlive a short-lived `memory notify`).

Immediate exit is safe: store writes are atomic renames, and flocks release on process exit.

## Validation

- Arming-rule unit tests; an integration test re-execs the test binary, SIGKILLs the parent, and asserts the armed child exits well under a second and releases a held `brainstore.AcquireFileLock` (the real lock implementation).
- `go test ./internal/cli ./internal/cli/internal/parentwatch` green; `gofmt -l -s` / `go vet` clean; cross-compiles for linux, windows, freebsd.

## Known limits

- A command that spawned a coding-agent child orphans it on watchdog exit — identical to today's SIGKILL behavior. `facts promote` spawns nothing.
- PDEATHSIG tracks the parent thread, not strictly the process (fallback path only).
- Dispatcher-side `Pdeathsig` on the plugin spawn (entire CLI repo) would be defense in depth; separate task.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF
)" 2>&1 | tail -1

input.command:
entire trail update 2715 --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Why

A customer runs many agents against one shared brain. Their prompt hook killed `entire brain facts promote` after 4 seconds with SIGKILL. SIGKILL to the `entire` CLI cannot be forwarded, so the plugin child reparented to pid 1 and held `locks/write.lock` for its full runtime (20 s to 1.5 min). Every concurrent reader failed `brain_locked`. SIGTERM was already covered by forwarding; SIGKILL was the gap.

## What changed

- New package `internal/cli/internal/parentwatch`. `Arm()` (called from `cli.Execute`) registers an OS parent-exit watch synchronously; one goroutine blocks on it and exits with one stderr line when it fires. No timers, no polling. Platform watchers: kqueue `NOTE_EXIT` (darwin), `pidfd_open` + `poll` (linux), `OpenProcess` + `WaitForSingleObject` (windows).
- Linux falls back to `PR_SET_PDEATHSIG` on any `pidfd_open` failure — ENOSYS (kernel < 5.3), EPERM (seccomp), ESRCH — since `prctl` works in the same sandboxes that block `pidfd_open`.
- A ppid re-check after registration closes the race where the parent dies before the watcher exists.
- The wait reports true only for an observed parent exit. Registration or wait failures with a live parent degrade to no watchdog; the watchdog can never kill a process whose parent is alive.
- Exemptions: no arming when initial ppid is 1 (launchd/systemd daemon) or when `ENTIRE_BRAIN_DETACHED=1` is set. Both detach paths set the marker: `spawnDetached` (setup backfill; `daemon-reregister`, whose parent dies by design under `launchctl bootout`) and `launchDetachedSelf` via `memoryWorkerChildEnvironment` (memory workers, which must outlive a short-lived `memory notify`).

Immediate exit is safe: store writes are atomic renames and flocks release on process exit. An aborted mutation loses only its batch.

## Validation

- Unit tests for the arming rules and the detached child environment; an integration test re-execs the test binary as parent and armed child, SIGKILLs the parent, and asserts the child exits well under a second and releases a held `brainstore.AcquireFileLock` (the real lock implementation).
- `go test ./internal/cli ./internal/cli/internal/parentwatch` green (232 s / 0.2 s).
- `gofmt -l -s` and `go vet` clean; cross-compiles for linux, windows, and freebsd (no-op fallback) pass.

## Known limits

- A command that spawned a coding-agent child orphans it on watchdog exit — identical to today's SIGKILL behavior, so no regression. The customer's failing command (`facts promote`) spawns no subprocesses.
- The PDEATHSIG fallback tracks the parent thread, not strictly the process (documented in the code).
- Dispatcher-side `Pdeathsig` on the plugin spawn (entire CLI repo) would be defense in depth; separate task.

Recorded design decision: Brain fact `fact:9c49fbb9132406a0a692e857` (branch `evisdren/brain_locked-write.lock-fix`); the full four-cause customer diagnosis is `fact:1d10ce176f39425716a28b6e`.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF
)" 2>&1 | tail -2

content.text:
Review done, fixes implemented, finding resolved. The fixes are **uncommitted in the working tree** (the findings skill leaves them for your review) — say the word and I commit and push them to the trail/PR.

## Findings and what happened to each

**[blocking] internal/cli/memory_cmd.go:129 — second detach path missed; watchdog would kill memory workers** (altitude agent, verified). `launchDetachedSelf` re-execs the plugin as a `memory worker --once` that must outlive the short-lived `memory notify` parent — its own comment says so. It does not go through `spawnDetached`, so it never got the exemption marker. **Fixed:** `memoryWorkerChildEnvironment` (the shared env builder for both of its callers) now sets `ENTIRE_BRAIN_DETACHED=1`; test extended first and watched fail. This was a real regression my original change would have shipped.

**[important] watch_darwin/linux/windows — degrade-path `select {}` can crash a healthy process.** A permanently Go-blocked goroutine trips the runtime's all-goroutines-asleep detector if nothing else is in a syscall. **Fixed:** the platform `wait` now returns `bool` (true only for an observed parent exit); `Arm` exits only on true, and all four `select {}` hangs are gone. The degrade rule now lives in one place.

**[low, trail finding 01M6CSRYH2FF1FDADFMGZVWVMT] watch_linux.go:19 — PDEATHSIG fallback only on ENOSYS.** Valid: seccomp-filtered containers return EPERM for `pidfd_open` while `prctl` still works. **Fixed:** the fallback now runs on any `pidfd_open` failure; `Arm`'s ppid re-check still covers the parent-already-dead case. **Resolved on the trail.**

**[nit, fixed] Simplification and reuse:** `spawnDetached` uses stdlib `cmd.Environ()` instead of the hand-rolled copy; `shouldArm` takes the env value instead of a lookup function; the darwin/linux EINTR loops share one `waitReady` helper; the integration test now holds the real `brainstore.AcquireFileLock` (what the customer bug was actually about), uses `brainstore.ProcessAlive`, and pins XDG roots like every sibling package.

**Skipped, deliberately:** netpoller-based waiting (saves one pinned OS thread; long-lived processes never arm, not worth the complexity), `base.EnvBool` for the marker (would drag the `tui` dependency into a leaf package), a generic env-replace helper (`os/exec` already resolves duplicate keys in favor of the last entry), and a session-leader (`Getsid`) exemption — the env marker now covers both detach paths on all platforms, and the recorded design keeps it as the portable contract.

## Validation

- Full `go test ./internal/cli ./internal/cli/internal/parentwatch`: green (232 s / 0.2 s).
- `gofmt -l -s` and `go vet` clean; cross-compiles pass for linux, windows, freebsd.

## Housekeeping

- Trail description updated to the post-fix state: https://entire.com/gh/entireio/-/trails/2715
- The auto-created shadow PR #584 had the branch name as its title and a placeholder body; it now has a real title and a cold-reader body (hidden Entire marker preserved).

**Assessment: approve after these fixes land.** The one item that genuinely mattered was the memory-worker regression — worth remembering that "detached" has two spawn paths in this codebase.
